scribe_response.text: Tell me about your first job. My first real job was at a pump manufacturing works in Coimbatore, in nineteen seventy-five. I was twenty-three years old, with a freshly printed degree and a very serious moustache. The works made centrifugal pumps for farmers, and the main shed echoed like a cathedral full of hammers. My title was uh junior design engineer, which meant that I did whatever the seniors preferred not to do. On my first morning the chief draughtsman handed me a pencil and a pile of worn drawings. He told me to check every dimension uh against a sample casting on the bench. I measured, I measured with a vernier caliper, and I found a mistake, a mistake in the very first drawing. The shaft diameter was off by two um tenths of a millimetre, and the casting had been poured wrongly for years. He looked at me for a long moment and then said that I might stay. I lived in a rented room above a tea shop, ten minutes by foot from the gate. The landlady was a retired nurse who served me idli every morning uh and charged very little. Mister Raghavan, the owner, walked the shed every morning at seven. He knew every worker by name and asked after their children. What happened next? My salary was four hundred and fifty rupees a month, um and I sent a quarter of it home. On Sundays the whole compound was silent, and I enjoyed that stillness. My mother wrote to ask whether I was eating enough. Each evening I walked back past the lathe shop and watched the apprentices sweep up the bright metal curls. I learned more from those men than from many professors, because they had skills in their fingertips. A foreman named Subramaniam taught me how to listen to a bearing and hear when it was tired. He held a long steel rod against the um housing and pressed the other end to his ear. I tried it dozens of times before I could hear the faint grinding he described. Eventually I did hear it, and he clapped me on the shoulder as though I had passed a great examination. We built a test rig for the pumps, with a glass tank and a row of pressure gauges. I was put in charge of it, and I took the role extremely seriously. Every pump um that left the works carried my initials on a small tag, which made me prouder um than a medal. There was one difficult customer, a landowner from Palakkad who returned a pump three times. Can you tell me more about that? Each time I travelled to his farm and found nothing wrong uh except that his well had dropped. Finally I explained the water level to him with a diagram drawn in the dust. He laughed, paid for a longer suction pipe, and sent me home with uh a sack of jaggery. Life in Coimbatore was quiet, and my entertainment was a weekly cricket match on a dusty ground. We played with a taped tennis ball, and I bowled slow spin that confused no one. After the match we um drank sweet tea from glasses at a roadside stall. The works taught me patience and the dignity of ordinary machines. I also discovered that a well made thing gives its maker a private satisfaction. After three years I began to feel restless, as if the shed had become too small. A senior colleague mentioned that engineers were wanted in the Gulf, where the coastal plants needed careful hands. I wrote a letter that evening, in my neat schoolmaster's handwriting, and posted it, it the next morning. Six months later an answer came, and my whole life turned on that single envelope. I will always be grateful to the old pump works for giving me my footing. Even now, when I hear a pump humming in a building, I stop to listen.
